title: Locke's Political Philosophy
orientation: Russell turns from Locke's epistemology to his Two Treatises on Government (1689-90), the founding texts of philosophical liberalism. The chapter traces Locke's demolition of Filmer's divine-right, hereditary theory of monarchy; his substitute account of a 'state of nature' governed by natural law; his social-contract theory of legitimate government; his controversial doctrine of property; and his theory of checks and balances -- while repeatedly showing how deeply these doctrines rest on unexamined theological premises and an unquestioned reverence for property.
historical_background: Locke wrote his two Treatises on Government in 1689-90, immediately after the Revolution of 1688. The First Treatise refutes Sir Robert Filmer's Patriarcha (published 1680, written under Charles I), which derived royal authority from Adam's God-given patriarchal power. The Second Treatise develops Locke's own positive theory: government originates in a social contract among free and equal individuals emerging from a pre-political 'state of nature.' Russell situates these doctrines against the English Civil War, the execution of Charles I, the conflict between king, aristocracy, and rising merchant class, and the enclosure movement that was, in Locke's own day, transforming English rural property relations even as Locke wrote as though peasant proprietorship were the norm.
philosophical_problems: Can hereditary political authority be justified by tracing it back to a divinely granted, Adam-derived patriarchal power (Filmer), or does heredity fail as a foundation for legitimate rule?
What is the 'state of nature,' and what natural law, if any, governs human conduct before or apart from civil government?
Can legitimate government be grounded in an actual or hypothetical social contract, and whose consent binds whom?
What is the proper basis and proper limits of private property, and does the labour theory of value adequately explain or justify it?
How should legislative, executive, and judicial power be separated to prevent tyranny, and what happens when these powers conflict?

philosophers_discussed.name: John Locke
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's primary subject: Russell reconstructs Locke's refutation of Filmer, his theory of the state of nature and natural law, his social contract doctrine, his theory of property (including the labour theory of value), and his doctrine of checks and balances, with sustained critical commentary throughout.

philosophers_discussed.name: Sir Robert Filmer
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Author of Patriarcha, the divine-right, hereditary theory of monarchy that Locke's First Treatise refutes; Russell examines Filmer's derivation of royal power from Adam's God-given paternal authority in some detail before turning to Locke's rebuttal.

philosophers_discussed.name: Thomas Hobbes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Contrasted with Locke on the state of nature (Hobbes's is a war of all against all) and on the social contract (in Hobbes, the sovereign is not a party to the contract and so acquires unlimited power, unlike in Locke's more limited, resistible government).

philosophers_discussed.name: Thomas Aquinas
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as an early source for both the concept of natural law ('every law framed by man bears the character of a law exactly to that extent to which it is derived from the law of nature') and a hint of social contract theory, and, via Tawney, as ancestor of the labour theory of value.

philosophers_discussed.name: Hugo Grotius
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as the source of the first serious development of social contract theory, building on the hint already present in Aquinas.

philosophers_discussed.name: Karl Marx
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Mentioned as (along with Ricardo) sometimes credited with the labour theory of value, which Russell traces back through Locke to Aquinas and the scholastics; quoted via Tawney as 'the last of the schoolmen.'

philosophers_discussed.name: David Ricardo
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named alongside Marx as a later exponent of the labour theory of value, which Russell shows Locke held 'in a vacuum, without hostility to any class,' unlike Ricardo (opposed to landowners) or Marx (opposed to capitalists).

philosophers_discussed.name: Montesquieu
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Credited with developing Locke's doctrine of the separation of powers further and with especially strong influence on the French constitutional tradition (e.g., the Constitution of 1871).

core_concepts.name: Filmer's patriarchal theory of divine right
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Sir Robert Filmer argued that kings rule because God originally gave Adam authority over the whole earth, which passed down through inheritance to modern monarchs -- so a king's power over subjects is really just an extension of a father's natural power over his children.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine, from Filmer's Patriarcha, that political power derives entirely from paternal authority: 'the source of regal authority is subjection of children to parents; ... the patriarchs in Genesis were monarchs; ... kings are the heirs of Adam, or at least are to be regarded as such; ... the natural rights of a king are the same as those of a father.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats this theory as historically important precisely because of how thoroughly and easily Locke demolished it, marking the effective end of hereditary divine right as a serious basis for European political legitimacy -- though Russell notes the same style of reasoning persisted, formally, in imperial Japan.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Patriarcha, published 1680 but written under Charles I, replying to 'subversive doctrines' already current before the Civil War.
examples: Filmer's claim that Noah allotted Africa, Asia, and Europe to Ham, Shem, and Japheth
The claim that 'the desire of liberty was the first cause of the fall of Adam'
Comparison to the pre-war Japanese imperial doctrine of descent from the Sun Goddess
objections: Locke: if parental power is the model, the mother's power should equal the father's
Locke: primogeniture is unjust as a principle, and paternal power is temporary and does not extend to life or property
Locke: Adam can have only one true heir, and no one knows who that is, so almost all monarchs would be usurpers on Filmer's own logic
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes the hereditary principle in politics had almost vanished by his own day (citing the fall of the Brazilian, Chinese, Russian, German, and Austrian monarchies), even as hereditary economic power (inherited wealth) survives largely unexamined.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Rooted in biblical genealogy (Adam, Noah, the patriarchs) and in the broader medieval battle between Church and State over the limits of kingly power.

core_concepts.name: The state of nature and natural law
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Locke imagines a condition before government existed, in which people lived under a 'law of nature' -- basically divine moral commands like 'do not harm others' life, health, liberty, or possessions' -- without any earthly ruler to enforce it. People in this state are free and equal, but because everyone must judge and enforce the law for themselves, conflicts are hard to resolve fairly.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Locke's 'state of nature' is 'men living together according to reason, without a common superior on earth, with authority to judge between them'; it is governed by a 'law of nature' consisting of divine commands (not human legislation), under which all individuals possess natural equality, natural freedom (bounded by the law of nature, not licence), and a natural right to self-defense and even to punish transgressors such as thieves or murderers.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This becomes the foundation for Locke's entire positive political theory: government exists specifically to remedy the great defect of the state of nature -- that in it, 'every man is the judge in his own cause.' Russell stresses that international relations between sovereign states remain, in Locke's own terms, in a state of nature to this day.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Second Treatise of Government; Russell notes it is 'in the main, not original,' echoing medieval scholastic natural law doctrine (e.g., Aquinas) more than it innovates.
examples: The natural right to kill a thief caught in the act of stealing
The Declaration of Independence's echo of Locke's 'life, health, liberty, or possessions'
The observation that independent states remain, toward each other, in a Lockean state of nature
objections: Russell notes an apparent inconsistency: Locke sometimes portrays the state of nature as populated by uniformly virtuous people, and at other times discusses how to deal with thieves and murderers within it
competing_positions: Hobbes's state of nature as a war of all against all, in which life is 'nasty, brutish, and short'
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly echoed in the American Declaration of Independence; Russell also reframes the doctrine in secular, untheological terms as a way of asking what retaliatory acts would be justified in the total absence of law and government.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: For Locke the law of nature is explicitly of divine origin, found ultimately in the Bible; Russell notes this theological basis is what modern secular liberalism has quietly dropped, leaving natural-rights talk 'destitute of clear logical foundation.'

core_concepts.name: The social contract
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Locke argues that legitimate government arises when free, equal individuals in the state of nature agree ('contract') to join together into one political community, giving up their private right to judge and punish wrongs in exchange for impartial, common laws and courts -- crucially, the government itself is also bound by this agreement and can be resisted if it breaks its side of the bargain.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Civil government originates when individuals consent to leave the state of nature by 'making one body politic'; unlike Hobbes's version, in which the sovereign is not a party to the contract and so gains unlimited power, in Locke's version government is itself a party to the contract, bound by it, and can be justly resisted if it fails to fulfil its part.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is the doctrinal core of Locke's 'more or less democratic' political theory -- though Russell stresses its democratic element was limited in practice, since Locke implicitly excluded women and the propertyless from full citizenship, and since the theory of legislative supremacy assumed government exists only 'for the public good' without ever specifying who judges what that good is.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Second Treatise of Government; Russell traces a hint of the doctrine back to Aquinas, with its 'first serious development' in Grotius.
examples: The requirement that 'the son must consent afresh to a compact made by his father,' which Russell notes is 'not very realistic'
The United States Constitution as a real historical attempt at a social contract, though many living under it never consented to it
objections: Russell: the social contract is 'mythical even when, at some former period, there actually was a contract,' since later generations never actually consent
Russell: Locke never explains why the consent of a bare majority (rather than every individual) should bind dissenters, e.g., pacifists taxed to fund war
competing_positions: Hobbes's contract, in which the sovereign stands outside the agreement and acquires unlimited authority
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Foundational to the American Constitution's structure of limited, resistible government and to the entire liberal-constitutionalist tradition.

core_concepts.name: Property and the labour theory of value
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Locke argued each person owns the product of their own labour, and that this is the main reason people form governments -- to protect their property. He also thought the value of most goods comes overwhelmingly from the labour put into them, and that people may fairly accumulate unlimited durable wealth (like gold), even though they may not hoard perishable goods (like plums) beyond what they can use.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Locke holds 'the great and chief end of men uniting into commonwealths ... is the preservation of their property,' that a man may own as much land as he can till (but no more), and that labour accounts for 'nine tenths' of the value of goods -- an early statement of the labour theory of value later associated with Ricardo and Marx, traceable, via Tawney, back through Locke to Aquinas and the scholastics' hostility to usury.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats Locke's property doctrine as deeply double-edged: it foreshadows developed capitalism's justification of accumulation (via imperishable metals and money) while also containing genuinely proto-socialist elements (labour as the true source of value, limits on landholding) that Locke never noticed were in tension with the England of his own day, where most agricultural land belonged to aristocrats, not labouring peasant-owners.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Second Treatise of Government, Section D ('Property'), as discussed by Russell; the labour theory's deeper roots lie in scholastic (Aquinas-derived) hostility to 'usury' and to speculative middlemen.
examples: Locke's rule that a man may own as much land as he can till, but no more
The 'plums' example: a man may not hoard more plums than his family can eat before they spoil, but may hoard unlimited gold and diamonds, since these do not perish
Locke's claim that uncultivated Indian land in America has almost no value, since value comes from labour
objections: Russell: Locke fails to notice that land can acquire value (e.g., from oil later found on it) without any labour being expended on it

Russell: the principle of a right to one's own produce becomes meaningless in an industrial system with complex divided labour (e.g., an assembly-line or railway worker's 'share' of output cannot be isolated)
Russell: Locke shows no awareness that the England of his own day, dominated by aristocratic landownership, was nothing like the peasant-proprietor system his principles implied
competing_positions: Later, more explicitly class-conscious versions of the labour theory of value in Ricardo (against landowners) and Marx (against capitalists)
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Traced forward by Russell (via Tawney) to Ricardo and ultimately Marx, whom Tawney calls 'the last of the schoolmen.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Rooted historically in scholastic condemnation of usury, later reversed as Protestant (especially Calvinist) merchant classes became lenders rather than borrowers.

core_concepts.name: Checks and balances (separation of powers)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Locke argued that legislative power (making laws) and executive power (enforcing them) should be kept separate, so that no single authority can both write self-serving laws and then enforce them without restraint. This idea later evolved, especially in the United States, into a full three-way division among legislature, executive, and judiciary.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Locke holds that 'the legislative and executive must be separate ... to prevent abuse of power,' with the legislative supreme but removable by the community; when executive and legislative conflict irreconcilably, Locke concedes there is, in a sense, 'no judge under Heaven,' meaning the dispute can ultimately only be settled by force.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This doctrine became a cornerstone of Anglo-American constitutionalism, most fully realized (per Russell) in the United States, where President, Congress, and Supreme Court are constitutionally independent of one another -- though Russell notes the doctrine largely broke down in Britain itself as the executive became, in practice, a parliamentary committee.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Second Treatise of Government, Section E; arose from English resistance to Stuart absolutism, especially Charles I's 1628-40 attempt to govern without summoning Parliament.
examples: Charles I's personal rule without Parliament (1628-40) as Locke's implicit target
The U.S. Supreme Court's power to nullify legislation, which Russell notes effectively makes it 'a branch of the legislature'
The American Civil War as a case where only military victory, not legal reasoning, settled a constitutional dispute (states' right to secede)
objections: Russell: Locke's principle that only 'unjust and unlawful' force may be resisted is useless without an agreed authority to judge what counts as unjust or unlawful
Russell: Locke says nothing about the judiciary as a separate branch, despite its being 'a burning question in his day'
competing_positions: The post-Locke British system, in which legislative and executive power became fused via cabinet government and party discipline
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Developed further by Montesquieu and embedded in the American Constitution and, at various points, in French constitutional arrangements (1871).

arguments.title: Locke's refutation of Filmer's hereditary/patriarchal monarchy
premises: If political authority derives from paternal authority, a mother's authority should equal a father's, yet Filmer's theory gives all power to the father/king alone.
Paternal power is inherently temporary (children grow up) and does not extend to life or property, unlike the absolute power Filmer attributes to kings.
Adam, even granting Filmer's premises, could have only one legitimate heir, and no one can identify who that heir is.
Primogeniture, needed to make heredity workable, is itself arbitrary and unjust.
arguments.conclusion: Heredity, traced back to Adam's supposed God-given authority, cannot be a coherent or defensible basis for legitimate political power; almost every actual monarch would, by Filmer's own logic, be a usurper.
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this as an 'easy task' for Locke: the First Treatise systematically shows that Filmer's premises, taken seriously, undermine rather than support the position they are meant to defend.
implications: Clears the ground for Locke's own positive, contractual theory of government in the Second Treatise
Marks, in Russell's account, the effective philosophical end of hereditary divine right as a serious European doctrine

arguments.title: Government as remedy for the defects of the state of nature
premises: In the state of nature, every individual has the natural right to judge and punish violations of natural law against themselves.
This means every person is 'the judge in his own cause,' which is inherently biased and unreliable, especially where the wrongdoer is powerful.
A neutral, common authority could adjudicate disputes far more fairly than each individual acting alone.
arguments.conclusion: Rational individuals in the state of nature would agree ('contract') to establish civil government, surrendering their private right of judgment and punishment to a common, impartial authority, in exchange for the preservation of their lives, liberties, and property.
arguments.explanation: This is the structural core of the Second Treatise. Russell notes that Locke's government, unlike Hobbes's, remains bound by the contract and can be resisted if it fails to secure the very goods (especially property) for which it was instituted.
objections: Absolute monarchy fails to solve the problem it claims to solve, since a monarch judging his own disputes with subjects is still, in effect, in a state of nature relative to them -- Locke's image: better to be 'devoured by lions' than protected from polecats and foxes only to be at the mercy of an absolute king
implications: Justifies resistance to tyrannical or contract-breaking government
Underlies later doctrines of limited, constitutional government

arguments.title: The labour theory of value
premises: Uncultivated land, such as that occupied but not farmed by American Indians, has 'almost no value.'
The same land, once laboured upon (cleared, planted, cultivated), acquires substantial value.
Generalizing, roughly nine-tenths of the value of any product can be attributed to the labour expended on it.
arguments.conclusion: Labour, not raw natural resources or land itself, is the primary source of economic value, and it is on this basis that individuals acquire a just property right in what they produce.
arguments.explanation: Russell traces this doctrine's genealogy through Tawney back to Aquinas and scholastic hostility to speculative gain, and forward to Ricardo and Marx, noting Locke is unusual among labour-theory advocates in holding the doctrine 'in a vacuum, without hostility to any class.'
objections: Land can acquire value without labour (e.g., a desert plot later found to sit atop oil)
The theory becomes unworkable once production is industrial and collective, since no individual's 'share' of a complex product (like a Ford car or railway freight) can meaningfully be isolated
implications: Motivates, in later thinkers, more explicitly class-based and eventually socialist critiques of property distribution that Locke himself never drew

arguments.title: The critique of Locke's theory of taxation and majority consent
premises: Locke holds that government may take no part of a person's property without that person's own consent.
Yet Locke also holds that taxation is legitimate so long as the majority of citizens (via their representatives) consents to it.
No principled bridge is given from 'every man's consent is required' to 'majority consent suffices,' beyond the fictional device of the social contract.
In practice, most people never had any real choice about which state they belong to, and citizenship is rarely, if ever, genuinely voluntary.
arguments.conclusion: Locke's justification of taxation by majority rule is not actually derivable from his individualist premises about property and consent, and rests on an unexamined, largely mythical notion of tacit consent.
arguments.explanation: Russell presses this with the example of a pacifist compelled to help fund a war through taxation: 'With what justice can you be compelled to submit to this?' -- a question he judges Locke's own principles cannot satisfactorily answer.
implications: Exposes a persistent tension in liberal theory between individual consent and majority rule that remains unresolved in later constitutional thought

key_distinctions: State of nature vs. state of war (Locke insists these are near opposites, against Hobbes)
Legislative power vs. executive power vs. judicial power
Real/nominal essence applied to property: labour-derived value vs. inherited/hereditary property
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Locke's natural law doctrine largely repeats medieval scholastic teaching, especially Aquinas's view that human law is only truly law insofar as it derives from natural law; his social contract theory develops a hint already present in Aquinas and given 'first serious development' by Grotius; his labour theory of value likewise descends, via Tawney's account of scholastic economic thought, from Aquinas's hostility to usurious, unproductive gain.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Locke's contract theory and separation-of-powers doctrine directly shape the American Constitution (refined by Montesquieu) and the Declaration of Independence's language of natural rights; the labour theory of value is carried forward by Ricardo and then Marx, whom Tawney calls 'the last of the schoolmen'; Russell also traces a longer genealogical line from Locke through Bentham and the philosophical Radicals to (eclectically) Marx himself.
political_social_context: Written to justify the Revolution of 1688 against the divine-right absolutism associated with the Stuarts, Locke's political philosophy reflects England's three-way struggle between monarchy, aristocracy, and the rising commercial middle class; Russell traces its later fate through the American and French constitutional traditions, the nineteenth-century enclosure movement (which contradicted Locke's peasant-proprietor assumptions), the industrial revolution (which outstripped Locke's individualist property theory), and the twentieth-century rise of dictatorships following the collapse of hereditary monarchy across Europe.
religion_science_culture_context: Locke's state of nature and natural law rest explicitly on theological premises (divine commands, humans as 'God's property'), and Russell notes the multiplicity of English religious sects, combined with the king's dual and inconsistent religious role as head of both the Church of England and the (Calvinist) Church of Scotland, materially undermined divine-right theories of kingship in England.
russell_presentation: Russell narrates Locke's political philosophy as a decisive, historically triumphant but philosophically uneven achievement. He first walks through Locke's comparatively effortless demolition of Filmer's patriarchal divine right, noting the peculiar historical circumstances (religious plurality, three-way conflict of king/aristocracy/middle class) that made England ready to abandon hereditary theories of legitimacy while Filmer-like reasoning persisted, in Russell's own time, in imperial Japan. He then reconstructs Locke's state of nature and natural law doctrine, stressing its debt to scholasticism and its shaky, largely theological foundations, before turning to the social contract, which Russell treats as historically fictional but not therefore useless as a normative device. The chapter's longest and most pointed criticism falls on Locke's theory of property: Russell shows how Locke's peasant-proprietor assumptions were already obsolete in his own day, how the labour theory of value cannot survive industrial production, and how Locke's 'worship of property' drove him to some of his 'oddest' and least defensible conclusions (e.g., that a monarch might justly flog soldiers but not fine them). Finally, Russell traces the doctrine of checks and balances from its origins in resistance to Stuart absolutism through to its fullest expression in the U.S. Constitution, closing with the observation that Locke's whole framework, built for individual citizens, has become increasingly inadequate to an age of organizations, corporations, and nation-states -- a problem Russell suggests can only be solved by an eventual 'international Social Contract.'
critical_context: Common scholarly criticism, echoed by Russell throughout: Locke's political philosophy takes for granted a world of independent, propertied individual citizens that was already becoming obsolete with the rise of industrial capital, corporations, and mass electorates; his implicit exclusion of women and the propertyless from full citizenship, and his failure to notice the gap between his peasant-proprietor property theory and the aristocratic landholding of his own England, are frequently cited limitations. Later development: Russell also flags Locke's theory as a direct ancestor, via the labour theory of value, of both classical (Ricardian) political economy and Marxist economics -- an unusual dual legacy for a theory originally devised, in Russell's account, without any particular class animus.
key_takeaways: Locke's First Treatise refutes Filmer's patriarchal, hereditary theory of divine-right monarchy by showing its internal inconsistencies (e.g., an unidentifiable 'true heir' of Adam, and unjustified primogeniture).
Locke's 'state of nature' is governed by a divinely grounded natural law and is explicitly not, contra Hobbes, a state of war -- but Russell notes real inconsistencies in how Locke describes it.
Civil government arises, for Locke, from a social contract in which government itself is bound by the agreement and can be resisted if it fails to protect life, liberty, and especially property.

Locke's theory of property, including an early labour theory of value, foreshadows both capitalist and (unintentionally) socialist economic thought, but assumes a pre-industrial world of independent peasant-proprietors.

Locke's doctrine of separated legislative and executive powers, refined by Montesquieu, became the constitutional basis of the United States, though it decayed in Britain itself as cabinet government fused the two.

Russell argues Locke's individualist framework is increasingly outmatched by an age of large organizations and nation-states, and anticipates that only an eventual international social contract could restore its relevance.
study_notes:
Read this chapter as a single sustained argument in five stages, each building on the last: (1) clear away the false, hereditary/divine-right foundation of political authority (the critique of Filmer); (2) establish what human life and rights would look like with no government at all (the state of nature and natural law); (3) explain how and why people would rationally leave that condition for civil society (the social contract); (4) explain what, above all, that society exists to protect (property, including the labour theory of value); and (5) explain how to structure government so that it does not itself become a new tyrant (checks and balances).

Pay special attention to where Russell inserts his own critical voice rather than simply reporting Locke. He is consistently sympathetic to Locke's historical achievement -- ending divine right, establishing resistance theory, shaping the American Constitution -- while being sharply critical of specific arguments: the mythical character of any real 'consent' to a social contract; the unworkability of the labour theory of value under industrial conditions; and the unexplained leap from 'no taxation without individual consent' to 'majority consent suffices.' A recurring theme worth tracking across the whole chapter is property: it motivates the formation of government in the first place, yet Locke's assumptions about property (peasant proprietorship, land you can personally till) were already being overtaken by enclosure and industrial capitalism even as he wrote.

Finally, notice the chapter's closing move: Russell extends Locke's own logic to argue that, since sovereign states remain (by Locke's own definition) in a 'state of nature' toward one another, a stable peace requires something like an international social contract -- a strikingly modern application of a seventeenth-century framework, written by Russell in the shadow of the Second World War.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Sir Robert Filmer's book arguing that kings inherit their authority from Adam, the first father, making royal power a form of paternal power.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Filmer's 1680 treatise grounding absolute monarchical authority in the patriarchal power God is said to have granted Adam over all his descendants.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Locke's imagined condition of human life before any government existed, in which people are free and equal but must enforce right and wrong themselves.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A pre-political condition, governed by divinely sanctioned natural law rather than human legislation, in which individuals possess natural liberty, equality, and the right to defend themselves and punish wrongdoers.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: For Locke, a set of moral rules given by God (like 'don't harm others') that apply even without any human government to enforce them.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Locke's term for divinely grounded moral obligations binding all rational persons in the state of nature, independent of positive (human-made) law.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that government is legitimate only because people have agreed, implicitly or explicitly, to form a political community together.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The doctrine that civil government originates in, and derives its authority from, the consent of those governed, who agree to leave the state of nature and form 'one body politic.'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that something's economic value comes mainly from the work put into making or improving it, not from the raw material alone.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The doctrine, traced by Russell from Aquinas through Locke to Ricardo and Marx, that the value of a product is (largely) determined by the labour expended in producing it.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Splitting government into separate branches (like lawmaking and law-enforcing) so that no one part gets too much power.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The doctrine, formulated by Locke and developed further by Montesquieu, that legislative, executive, and (later) judicial functions of government should be institutionally separated to prevent abuse of power.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The rule that the eldest child (usually eldest son) automatically inherits everything.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: An inheritance rule Locke criticizes as unjust, and as an unavoidable but arbitrary consequence of grounding legitimate authority on heredity.
related_concepts: Filmer's patriarchal theory of divine right

questions.prompt: What is Sir Robert Filmer's basic argument, in Patriarcha, for why kings should be obeyed?
questions.answer: That God originally gave Adam authority over the whole earth and all his descendants, that this authority passed down by inheritance, and that modern kings either are, or are to be treated as, Adam's rightful heirs -- so royal power is essentially an extension of paternal power.
questions.explanation: Filmer's theory is the target of Locke's First Treatise on Government.

questions.prompt: Which philosopher held that, unlike Locke's version, the sovereign is not a party to the social contract and therefore acquires unlimited authority?
questions.explanation: In Hobbes's version, citizens contract among themselves to hand over all power to a sovereign who stands outside the agreement, unlike Locke's contract, in which government itself is bound and resistible.

questions.prompt: According to Locke, what is the 'great and chief end' for which people unite into commonwealths and institute government?
questions.explanation: This quotation is central to Russell's discussion of how deeply property concerns shape Locke's entire political theory.

questions.prompt: Compare Locke's and Hobbes's conceptions of the state of nature.
questions.answer: Hobbes's state of nature is a war of all against all, in which life is nasty, brutish, and short, justifying an absolute, unlimited sovereign. Locke's state of nature is, in his own words, nearly the opposite of a state of war -- a condition of liberty, equality, and general (though imperfect) obedience to natural law, justifying only a limited, contract-bound, resistible government.
questions.explanation: Russell notes Locke's account is directed, in places, explicitly against Hobbes.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's objection to Locke's justification of taxation by majority consent.
questions.answer: Locke holds that government cannot take any part of a person's property without that person's own consent, yet also holds that majority consent to taxation suffices. Russell argues Locke gives no principled bridge between these two claims (beyond the fictional social contract), and that in practice most people never really chose their citizenship or consented to be taxed -- raising the unanswered question of what justifies compelling, say, a pacifist to fund a war through taxes.
questions.explanation: This is one of Russell's sharpest critical arguments in the chapter.

questions.prompt: What example does Locke use to argue that gold and diamonds may be accumulated without limit, unlike perishable goods such as plums?
questions.answer: That plums will go bad before a family can eat them if hoarded beyond need, but gold and diamonds, being imperishable, may be lawfully accumulated in any quantity.
questions.explanation: Russell singles this out as one of Locke's odder arguments, noting Locke overlooks that plums could simply be sold before spoiling.

questions.prompt: How does the doctrine of checks and balances fare differently in Britain versus the United States, according to Russell?
questions.answer: In the United States, the President, Congress, and Supreme Court remain constitutionally independent of one another, the fullest application of Locke's principle. In Britain, by contrast, the executive gradually became dependent on, and effectively a committee of, Parliament, so that legislative and executive power fused -- 'totally contrary to Locke's principles.'
questions.explanation: Russell traces this divergence through the history of cabinet government and party discipline.

flashcards.front: What book does Locke's First Treatise on Government refute?
flashcards.back: Sir Robert Filmer's Patriarcha, which grounds royal authority in Adam's inherited, God-given patriarchal power.

flashcards.front: What is Locke's definition of the 'state of nature'?
flashcards.back: Men living together according to reason, without a common superior on earth with authority to judge between them.

flashcards.front: What is the great and chief end of government, according to Locke?
How does Locke's social contract differ from Hobbes's?
flashcards.back: In Locke's version, government itself is a party to the contract and can be resisted if it breaks the agreement; in Hobbes's version, the sovereign stands outside the contract and gains unlimited power.

flashcards.front: What natural right does Locke say every person has in the state of nature?
flashcards.back: The right to defend themselves and their property, and to punish attacks against themselves, even by death.

flashcards.front: According to Locke's labour theory of value, what fraction of a product's value comes from labour?
What is Russell's objection to Locke's labour theory of value regarding land?
flashcards.back: Land can acquire value (e.g., if oil is discovered on it) without any labour being expended on it -- a case Locke does not consider.

flashcards.front: What did Locke say about the imperishability of gold and diamonds?
flashcards.back: That, unlike perishable goods such as plums, gold and diamonds may be justly accumulated without limit because they do not spoil.

flashcards.front: What historical figure is Locke's chapter on checks and balances implicitly responding to?
flashcards.back: Charles I, who tried to govern England without summoning Parliament from 1628 to 1640.

flashcards.front: Who further developed Locke's doctrine of the separation of powers, especially influencing France?
Which branch of government does Russell note Locke says almost nothing about?
flashcards.back: The judiciary, despite it being a 'burning question' in Locke's own day.

flashcards.front: What example does Russell give of Locke's political theory being outstripped by industrial and corporate power?
flashcards.back: The rise of vast corporations wielding economic power far beyond anything Locke imagined for individual citizens.

flashcards.front: What does Russell say still exists in a Lockean 'state of nature,' even today?
flashcards.back: The relations between independent sovereign states, absent an international government.

flashcards.front: Who does Tawney credit as 'the last of the schoolmen,' in the lineage of the labour theory of value?

quiz.prompt: Locke's First Treatise on Government is primarily a refutation of whom?
quiz.explanation: Locke's First Treatise refutes Filmer's Patriarcha and its patriarchal, hereditary defense of divine-right monarchy.
quiz.related_concept: Filmer's patriarchal theory of divine right

quiz.prompt: According to Locke, the 'great and chief end' of forming civil government is:
quiz.explanation: Locke states repeatedly that government exists chiefly to preserve property.
quiz.related_concept: Property and the labour theory of value

quiz.prompt: True or False: In Locke's version of the social contract, the government itself is bound by the contract and can be justly resisted if it breaks it.
quiz.explanation: Unlike Hobbes's sovereign (who stands outside the contract), Locke's government is a party to the contract and subject to resistance if it fails its obligations.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of Locke's objections to Filmer's hereditary theory?
options: A mother's power should equal a father's if parental power is the basis of authority
Adam's true heir cannot be identified
Paternal power is temporary and does not extend to property
Heredity guarantees wise and virtuous rulers
quiz.explanation: Locke never claims heredity guarantees wisdom or virtue; his objections concern the internal incoherence of Filmer's derivation of authority.
quiz.related_concept: Filmer's patriarchal theory of divine right

quiz.prompt: In Locke's state of nature, the great defect that government remedies is that every man is ____ in his own cause.
quiz.explanation: Locke's core argument for government is that, absent a common authority, each individual must judge and enforce their own rights, which is inherently unreliable.
quiz.related_concept: The state of nature and natural law

quiz.prompt: Russell's objection to Locke's account of taxation centers on:
options: The unfairness of taxing the rich
The unexplained leap from 'individual consent is required' to 'majority consent suffices'
Locke's opposition to any taxation whatsoever
Locke's support for taxation without representation
quiz.explanation: Russell argues Locke provides no principled justification for why majority consent should bind individuals (such as pacifists) who did not personally consent.

quiz.prompt: Russell traces the labour theory of value, via Tawney, back to which earlier source?
quiz.explanation: Russell cites Tawney's account of scholastic economic doctrine, opposed to speculative and usurious gain, as the ultimate ancestor of the labour theory of value running through Locke to Ricardo and Marx.
quiz.related_concept: Property and the labour theory of value

quiz.prompt: True or False: Russell argues that Locke's doctrine of checks and balances found its fullest application in Britain rather than the United States.
quiz.explanation: Russell states the doctrine found its fullest application in the United States; in Britain, the executive and legislative powers gradually fused through cabinet government.

quiz.prompt: Match each thinker to their relationship to Locke's political philosophy: (1) Grotius, (2) Montesquieu, (3) Marx.
options: (1) First serious developer of social contract theory; (2) Developed the separation of powers further; (3) Later exponent of the labour theory of value
(1) Refuted Locke's contract theory; (2) Opposed checks and balances; (3) Rejected the labour theory of value
(1) Wrote Patriarcha; (2) Was Locke's patron; (3) Founded liberalism
(1) Was a Tory historian; (2) Opposed the American Constitution; (3) Agreed entirely with Ricardo
quiz.explanation: Grotius gave social contract theory its first serious development; Montesquieu extended the separation of powers (especially influencing France); Marx, per Tawney, is 'the last of the schoolmen' in the labour-theory lineage.
quiz.related_concept: Property and the labour theory of value

essay_prompts.prompt: Analyze Locke's refutation of Filmer's patriarchal theory of divine right. Which of Locke's specific objections do you find most decisive, and why?
rubric: Accurate summary of at least three of Locke's objections

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Russell's claim that Locke's social contract is 'mythical' even where a historical contract (such as the U.S. Constitution) actually existed. Does this undermine the contract's usefulness as a justification for political obligation?
rubric: Consideration of the U.S. Constitution example
Discussion of tacit vs. explicit consent

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Locke's labour theory of value with its later development in Ricardo and Marx. Why does Russell suggest Locke held the theory 'in a vacuum, without hostility to any class,' unlike his successors?
rubric: Accurate statement of Locke's version of the theory
Accurate contrast with Ricardo's and Marx's class-inflected versions
Discussion of the theory's viability under industrial conditions
